finding.claim: dropTable ignores the error returned by Authorize, so any caller can run DROP TABLE with an attacker-chosen table name (missing authorization). The unsanitized table name in the same statement also allows SQL injection.
finding.source: Any HTTP client reaching /admin/drop, including one without the 'dba' role. The table name comes from the form value 't'.

trace.note: /admin/drop is registered with dropTable, with no auth middleware
userFrom obtains the user from the request context
Authorize(u, "dba") returns an error for non-dba users, but the result is discarded
The SQL string is built by concatenating r.FormValue("t") and passed to runSQL

finding.guards_checked: Authorize is called but its error is not checked. There is no middleware, as the handler is registered directly on the default mux. The table name is not validated or allowlisted. The vacuum handler at api.go:33 checks the error correctly, which shows what the intended guard looks like.

verdict.guard_found: Authorize(u, "dba") at api.go:26 is a bare statement whose returned error is discarded. There is no middleware and no table-name validation. The only other control is the type assertion in userFrom at api.go:22, which panics if no user is in the context. Nothing in this directory sets that value.
verdict.reason: api.go:26 discards the error from Authorize, so api.go:27 runs "DROP TABLE " + r.FormValue("t") for any caller whose request reaches the handler, and the handler is registered with no auth middleware at api.go:44. Caveat: nothing in this directory puts a "user" value in the context, so as written the type assertion at api.go:22 would panic for every request. That looks like an artifact of the snippet, and any upstream middleware that does set the user would leave non-dba users able to drop tables.
